This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within the linear span of known basis functions, we establish that the generalization error is bound by $\sigma(r)(\frac{\ln d}{n})^{1/2}$, where $\sigma$ is the condition number, $r$ is the ratio of basis functions to sample size, $d$ is the dimensionality, and $n$ is the sample size. This bound surpasses existing estimates by removing unnecessary restrictions on input domain size and basis function space, while also improving the dependence on sample size. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the neural network generalization performance matches the optimal rate in a standard regression task, thus validating the theoretical non-asymptotic analysis and enabling data-driven approaches for ground state computation. We examine a sequential migration-contagion process where migrants arrive at a new country and spread disease to non-migrant native individuals. Migrant health status is assumed to be drawn from a specific distribution, and they remain healthy until they contract the disease. Each migrant is considered a disease vector, and upon contracting the disease, they are removed from the population. To analyze this process, we develop a mathematical framework using generating functions and apply it to two specific scenarios: a basic SIR model and a SIR model with relaxation, both of which have been studied by Aral et al. Our results provide an exact expression for the probability distribution of native individuals remaining healthy or having contracted and recovered from the disease over time. We also derive time-evolution equations in a compact form and determine the asymptotic behavior of the system as it approaches a stationary state. Additionally, we calculate the average and variance of key performance metrics and verify numerical results by simulating different parameters. Notably, our findings indicate that the system's behavior can be divided into distinct regimes based on the parameter values. We also observe that the asymptotic system behavior is influenced by a specific parameter and that the system's behavior can be shifted left or right by adjusting this parameter. Our work can be extended to investigate the impact of multiple disease vectors on the system's behavior. We hope that our analysis will contribute to a better understanding of the interplay between migration and disease spread, ultimately informing policy decisions. The mathematical framework developed in this study can be applied to various other sequential processes. We plan to extend our model to incorporate multiple disease vectors in a forthcoming study. The recent discovery of multiple planetary systems with complex architectures, characterized by multiple transiting planets, has significant implications for our understanding of planetary formation. Specifically, the observation of non-random eclipse time variations in K2-138, caused by a 9-day gap in its planetary period, suggests the presence of a 3:2 mean motion resonance among its four inner planets. To verify this hypothesis, we conducted a statistical analysis of the eclipse times using the No-No Correlation test, confirming the existence of a 9-day period anomaly at a high level of confidence. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a second, shorter gap in the planetary periods at 54.5 days, indicating the presence of a fifth planet. The resulting orbital period ratios are in close agreement with theoretical predictions for a 3:2 resonance chain. However, the inclusion of the fifth planet does not improve the fit to the eclipse time data, casting doubt on its validity. In light of these findings, we recommend revisiting the K2-138 light curve to search for additional transits and improve the dynamical model of the system. Ultimately, our analysis provides strong evidence for the presence of a 3:2 resonance chain in K2-138, supported by a statistically significant test result of $2.98\sigma$. This finding serves as a foundation for future dynamical modeling and theoretical interpretations of this remarkable planetary system. As a result, we derive a pointwise description of the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial via the character of a module vector and provide an explanation for its non-negative integer values. Furthermore, we establish a commutative diagram involving the Whittaker functor, the Coaction Hopf algebra, the quantum affine algebra, and the general linear group $\mathrm{GL}_N(q)$. This diagram encapsulates the interplay between these entities and their respective actions and invariants. Specifically, the Whittaker functor is shown to be equivalent to a Drinfeld action on invariants, thereby generalizing the Gelfand--Graev modules for central covers and the Kashiwara--Okado module for the quantum affine algebra. As an additional outcome, we derive a commutative diagram involving the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial, the character of a module vector, and the Weyl multiplication. To simulate the formation of crystal-ice domains in hydrogen cyanide (HCN) ice, which is isomorphous with water ice, we conducted a series of $2\cdot10^9$ molecular dynamics simulations. These simulations started with a random initial configuration and applied thermal stress until the system reached equilibrium at $50$ K for various sizes of HCN clusters. We then analyzed the electronic structure and connectivity of the bonds using Pauling's criteria to identify crystalline regions. However, due to the limitations of the Pauling theory in distinguishing between different ice structures and the absence of a clear-cut definition of domain size, we instead employed a graph clustering approach based on molecular structure similarity. This method allowed us to accurately simulate the growth of domains in HCN at temperatures ranging from $40$ to $60$ K and compare our results with existing experimental and computational data on water ice. We found that, similar to water, the structure of HCN ice exhibits a first-order transition between liquid and crystalline phases, characterized by the formation of large crystal domains at higher temperatures. We also observed that the size of the domains in HCN is directly proportional to the size of the system, which is consistent with previous studies on water. However, unlike water, the domain structure in HCN is not uniform and exhibits irregular shapes and complex geometries. We attribute these differences to the distinct chemical properties of HCN and water, which affect their bonding patterns and arrangement. These findings suggest that domain formation in HCN and other similar molecules follows a universal pattern that can be replicated through extensive simulations. These simulations can be scaled up to study the growth of domains in larger systems and the effects of external factors, such as radiation and atmospheric conditions, which are essential for understanding the astrochemical processes involved in the formation of complex molecules. These formulas are then used to present a unified approach to factoring variants of Chebyshev polynomials, with a key theorem providing a criterion for irreducibility over the rationals. Additionally, some factorization methods for variants of Chebyshev polynomials are outlined. Finally, a computational framework for these polynomials is described. This review explores the theoretical underpinnings and applications of the Zeroing Neural Network (ZNN), a time-varying matrix equation solver that employs a predictive computation approach. The derivation of ZNN's dynamic models is discussed along with the establishment of their continuous-discrete frameworks and the critical roles of the state matrix in their design. Furthermore, an analysis of ZNN's dynamic behaviors, including stability and convergence, is provided, accompanied by an examination of the impact of initial conditions on solution accuracy. Lastly, various ZNN-based algorithms for addressing time-varying matrix problems are presented and assessed. Several real-world problems are chosen to demonstrate the efficacy of ZNN in tackling multibody dynamics, optimal control, adaptive filtering, and control problems involving systems with multiple input and output channels. The results of the presented examples not only validate the theoretical convergence of ZNN but also highlight its superior performance relative to alternative solvers. Ultimately, this review aims to facilitate the development of ZNN-based algorithms for addressing a broad range of time-varying matrix problems. As such, it is anticipated that this work will inspire the creation of novel ZNN applications and foster innovation in the field of predictive computations. The review concludes by identifying avenues for future research and potential extensions of the ZNN paradigm. The accompanying supplementary material can be accessed at the provided link.

A new deep neural network model, based on the biological properties of retinal ganglion cells' ON-OFF cells, is proposed for image classification tasks. This model, called CoSNet, replicates the ON-OFF center-surround receptive field of parvocellular and magnocellular ganglion cells. It consists of an initial convolutional layer with two sub-layers that mimic the center and surround components of the receptive field. We trained CoSNet on standard image datasets and found that it outperforms other neural networks in terms of accuracy. Additionally, we tested its ability to withstand noise by evaluating its performance on noisy images and found that it is more robust than the alternatives. We also analyzed the model's computational efficiency and found that it is comparable to or lower than that of the top-performing baseline model, depending on the specific architecture. We validated the model's effectiveness by applying it to image classification and image recognition tasks across different retinal ganglion cell types and found that it is generally more accurate than the alternatives. However, we did observe some cases of model bias, where the model performed better on images with certain ganglion cell types' characteristics and worse on those with opposing characteristics. We propose that this phenomenon may be due to the model's alignment with the brain's functional organisation and the prevalence of S-cones in the human retina. Overall, our findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating biological insights into neural network design in order to achieve superior performance. CoSNet has the potential to be a valuable tool for image classification and other tasks, as well as serving as a platform for the development of more accurate and efficient models of retinal processing. We have made the code for CoSNet available to the public, along with the data used in our experiments. The Set-Union Knapsack problem represents a challenging computational optimization task, where the goal is to determine the optimal combination of items from a list with the highest total value, while staying within a limit of storage capacity and not exceeding a specified total cost. This problem is a more complex variation of the traditional Knapsack problem. We propose an improved solution approach, building on the idea of a greedy algorithm and incorporating a local search mechanism to find better approximations. By reducing the problem to a series of smaller, interrelated problems and employing a rigorous exploration of possible combinations via a combinatorial local search algorithm, our method demonstrates the ability to find high-quality, nearly optimal solutions. Additionally, we demonstrate the flexibility of our approach by adapting it to solve another important optimization problem, the Budgeted Maximum Coverage task. Through comprehensive testing on a wide range of synthetic and real-world datasets, we showcase the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed algorithm, achieving an average 5.6% improvement in solution quality over existing state-of-the-art methods, while also significantly reducing computation time in many cases. Notably, our results show that the highest-quality solutions are found using a simple, efficient implementation of the combinatorial local search algorithm. Furthermore, when time is a limiting factor, a rapid and effective variant of the algorithm is able to find satisfactory solutions in a short period of time. Overall, our research culminates in the identification of a robust and versatile optimization solver, capable of handling a wide range of problem instances with ease. This solution approach is particularly useful for tackling various decision support and resource allocation challenges across a diverse array of fields and applications. As an example, it has the potential to be applied in the context of allocating resources to solve complex, multi-faceted problems. Moreover, our proposed algorithm is also suitable for addressing the Maximum Coverage problem in a distributed computing environment. Finally, our research highlights the importance of thorough testing and validation of optimization algorithms on a diverse set of problem instances to accurately assess their performance and efficiency. Moreover, our results demonstrate the value of employing a local search mechanism to further improve the solution quality of combinatorial optimization algorithms. In summary, our research aims to contribute significantly to the field of combinatorial optimization by proposing an efficient and effective solution approach that can be widely utilized in practice. Top tagging is a crucial strategy in the search for exotic particles that decay into top quarks. Recent studies have shown that machine learning techniques can significantly boost the identification of boosted top quarks. This thesis delves into the application of two machine learning methods, XTrim and a Boosted Tagger, to detect boosted top quarks. By applying these algorithms to simulated data, we explored their performance using three key variables: N-subjet N-1, N-2 trimming variables, and N-2 trimming top tagging discriminant. Our analysis revealed that XTrim outperforms the Boosted Tagger in most scenarios. To ensure the results can be used in practice, we developed a straightforward method to determine the efficiency of tagging for any set of N-2 trimming top tagger outputs. This approach is based on the concept of efficiency vectors and is defined as a linear combination of the original efficiency variable. This technique is versatile and can be applied to any top tagger, while also enabling the creation of a comprehensive lookup table for boosted top tagging. Finally, we employed the SHAP package to demonstrate how the tagging process can be broken down into the individual contributions of the three key variables. This analysis revealed that N-subjet N-1 remains the dominant variable throughout the N-2 trimming top tagger phase space. Our findings also show that the variable's importance peaks at N-2 trimming outputs below 0.7, indicating that the tagging process primarily relies on N-subjet information during this phase. Additionally, we observed that the remaining variable space, encompassed by N-2 trimming outputs above 0.7, is dominated by the N-2 trimming top tagger. This result suggests that the tagging process for these events is inherently more complex and relies on both N-subjet and trimming characteristics. This study's outcome may lead to further research into the application of machine learning techniques to disentangle these two variable categories. Ultimately, this analysis may facilitate the development of more targeted searches for exotic particles that decay into top quarks in the Standard Model or beyond. Hierarchical taxonomies are widely used for categorizing items and concepts in various applications. However, current approaches to automatic taxonomy expansion face limitations due to the linear representation of concepts in traditional space, which hinders the effective encoding of hierarchical structures. In contrast, hyperbolic embeddings better capture the hierarchical relationships between concepts, outperforming their counterparts in related tasks. Building upon this insight, we introduce HyperExpan, an algorithm for taxonomy expansion that leverages the advantages of hyperbolic representation learning. By incorporating an edge-aware loss function that prioritizes nearest neighbor edges, HyperExpan surpasses the performance of competing methods, which often rely on heuristics or ad-hoc techniques, to accurately predict unseen concepts in a node's neighborhood. Empirical evaluations across multiple taxonomy datasets validate the efficacy of HyperExpan, confirming its superiority over competing methods in both node classification and nearest neighbor prediction tasks. Notably, HyperExpan achieves a notable 6.5% improvement over the state-of-the-art in node classification, underscoring the benefits of hyperbolic representation learning for taxonomy expansion. The implementation of HyperExpan is publicly available at https://github.com/zy1995/HyperExpan. The accompanying code for reproducing the experimental results can be found at https://github.com/zy1995/HyperExpan-Reproduce. The data used in these experiments can be accessed at https://github.com/zy1995/Data. The findings of this study are further substantiated by an ablation study, demonstrating the relative contributions of various components in HyperExpan, including triplet-based edge-constrained training, edge-aware loss, and the choice of hyperbolic embedding model. Notably, incorporating the edge-aware loss function yields a significant 4.8% improvement in performance, while using the edge-constrained triplet-based training approach results in a 2.5% gain. The choice of hyperbolic embedding model, specifically the H2GAE model, is also found to contribute 1.8% to the overall performance of HyperExpan. The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of active debate. In this study, we focus on a well-established paramagnetic and superconducting LiFeAs system, which exhibits no magnetism or nematicity upon cooling. To investigate this, we employed an in situ high-pressure device to measure its electrical resistivity under various conditions, complemented by first-principles calculations and a mean-field theory simulation of electronic orbital ordering. Our results show that in LiFeAs, the orbital excitations do not have sufficient entropy to cause a structural and electronic phase transition similar to that observed in iron-based magnetic superconductors, even when subjected to high pressure. This implies that the presence of magnetic ions is a critical factor in the appearance of nematicity in these materials. Additionally, we found that the orbital ordering in LiFeAs is stabilized at an extremely low level, far below the estimated statistical equilibrium concentration, which supports our experimental findings and aligns with the idea that the orbital degrees of freedom in this system are over-constrained. This research sheds light on the intricate relationship between magnetism, nematicity, and superconductivity in iron-based superconductors. Furthermore, it provides valuable insights into the high-pressure physics of LiFeAs and offers a framework for understanding the relationship between these properties and the presence of magnetic ions in iron-based superconductors. Lastly, we discuss the potential applications of this framework in the study of other materials. The findings of this study are significant and have been thoroughly verified. However, they contradict some existing research on LiFeAs, which reported the occurrence of nematicity under high pressure. To resolve this discrepancy, we suggest that the reported nematic effect in LiFeAs is likely a result of contamination or an unintended contact in the experimental setup. This possibility is supported by our own high-pressure experiments on NaFeAs and FeSe, which also failed to exhibit nematicity. This study was performed with the necessary expertise and equipment, including in situ high-pressure devices, to conclusively rule out the presence of nematicity in LiFeAs. Our research provides new insights into the physics of iron-based superconductors and offers a new perspective on the relationship between orbital ordering, magnetism, and superconductivity in these materials. This paper introduces two alterations for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. The first variation involves employing a random vector of minimal weight t, rather than a t-error correcting code, as the challenge vector. Provided that t is less than (n - r)/2, this modification necessitates approximately $\mathcal{O}(t^2)$, rather than $\mathcal{O}(r^2)$, queries to recover the secret vector. The second modification combines a t-error correcting code with a (t+1)-error correcting code of equivalent length. As a result, an attacker attempting to generate a valid challenge vector must first compute a secret vector compatible with the combined code, which significantly increases the required query count to approximately $\mathcal{O}(2t+1)$. Theoretical analyses confirm that both modifications enhance the security of the underlying system. Furthermore, an experimental assessment of these changes using a C code implementation demonstrated that they offer practical advantages in terms of resistance to side-channel attacks. The findings suggest that systems with smaller lengths r, such as those with r=2048, are particularly well-suited to these modifications, which offer increased security without performance degradation. The resulting systems exhibit comparable or improved resistance to side-channel attacks compared to conventional ones, while maintaining a reasonable query count for the secret vector recovery. The authors propose that these modifications serve as a potential solution to the query bound attack problem in code-based cryptosystems. The detailed design of the modified system is presented in Section 2, and the theoretical and experimental outcomes are discussed in Section 3. The dictionary contains word-meaning pairs where each meaning is represented as a token. The PLM is then trained to predict not only the target token, but also the token representing the specified meaning. The training objectives include predicting the start and end positions of the target meaning as well as the target class itself. The experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT outperforms BERT in all tested NLP tasks, including word sense induction, sentiment analysis, and word sense label distribution analysis. Furthermore, we have made our dictionary available for download. The Dict-BERT model and the dictionary can be accessed through the link: https://github.com/whai362/Dict-BERT. The findings suggest that Dict-BERT is particularly effective for domain-specific and word sense related tasks. Lastly, we have observed that the tokenized meanings in the dictionary have become out of date due to the limited number of tokens allowed in the dictionary, which may hinder the performance of Dict-BERT. In cross-device federated learning, devices collaborate with a central server by exchanging data. This paper examines privacy risks in a specific scenario where devices train models locally using data from the central server and share updated parameters with the server. By reverse-engineering the server's model, adversaries can infer sensitive user information, even with encrypted data and a single batch attack. Performance-based experiments using convolutional neural networks and gradient-based attacks demonstrate that the attack is effective across various user counts, data sizes, and data types, and the risk increases with data sensitivity. Additionally, the study finds that the attack is more challenging with medical images and audio data, but the attack can be improved by combining these data types with other categories. Furthermore, the research shows that non-uniform user data distributions do not hinder the attack and that the primary factor affecting success is the data type, followed by user count and data size. These findings highlight the need for robust privacy protection in this context. Based on these results, the study proposes a metric to evaluate the vulnerability of user data and suggests several defense strategies to counteract the attack. By employing differential privacy, limiting user data transmission, and implementing a local data validation mechanism, the research demonstrates that these methods can effectively safeguard user data and prevent the attack. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the importance of developing secure and private vertical federated learning algorithms. The research code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuyao/Practical-Privacy-Attack-on-Vertical-Fed-Learn.

Document ranking with noise-labeled data poses a significant challenge, and conventional methods often fail to account for the diverse quality of these labels. In this research, we examine the concept of noise-labeled data collection through bag sampling, highlighting its characteristics that give rise to label noise. Additionally, we introduce a novel class-wise loss function to mitigate the impact of noisy labels, demonstrating its improved robustness in theory and experimental studies. The results indicate that our approach outperforms existing document ranking methods using noisy labels, with comparable performance when clean labels are used; notably, our approach shows resilience against varying levels of label noise. The proposed method has been successfully applied to BERT4OR, achieving state-of-the-art outcomes in offline and online ranking tasks. Notably, our approach exhibits strong adaptability when integrated with other ranking models. The research findings and code are openly accessible on GitHub, contributing to the advancement of noise-labeled data learning in information retrieval. The research also sheds light on the challenges and potential solutions associated with noise-labeled data collection. In response to this challenge, we propose an innovative approach, Informativeness-Ranked Pseudo-Labeling (IRPL), to enhance the quality of pseudo-labels produced by GNNs, thereby improving their performance even with a limited number of labels available. By leveraging the concept of label informativeness, which reflects the ease of prediction on a given node, given its neighbors' labels, and an efficient approximation method, IRPL achieves significant improvements over competing methods across three benchmark datasets. Specifically, IRPL achieves average performance boosts of 2.3% to 6.8% in terms of micro F1-score, thereby solidifying its status as a highly effective semi-supervised learning strategy for GNNs. Interestingly, the microwave conductivity can distinguish between various states of disorder and highlight the role of kinetic energy in driving superconductivity in cuprate materials. Overall, the findings demonstrate that cuprate superconductors in the normal phase exhibit complex energy and temperature dependent transport behavior, characterized by distinct microwave conductivity responses. These observations can be utilized to explore the disorder-dependent behavior of superconducting materials and identify potential order-parameter driven states in cuprate materials and other systems. One of the widely used data analysis techniques in big data is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). This can be a significant issue in large-scale computations due to the time and resources required for communication. Notably, CommNet has been able to achieve a 3.5 times speedup in the training time for the CommNet-S1 implementation compared to the baseline SGD method, while also yielding comparable classification accuracy. Characterized by the electron cyclotron current drive's (ECD) unique signature and distinct from other edge turbulence features, PTMs have a narrower frequency range of 20-40 MHz and exhibit radial persistence. The findings suggest that a Poisson degree distribution leads to a collective output frequency equal to the driving frequency, while distributions lacking Poisson characteristics yield more complex results. Specifically, power law degree distributions with a gamma index less than one result in a lower output frequency, and as gamma approaches zero, this decrease becomes more pronounced, leading to output frequencies that may split into multiple components. Conversely, power law distributions with a gamma index greater than one yield a higher output frequency, and increasing gamma's value leads to this higher frequency. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a comprehensive dataset designed to support the development of dexterous robotic grasping methods. Unlike existing datasets that focus on specific objects like household items or use simplified simulation models, DexGraspNet encompasses a broad range of products from online retailers with complex geometries. It features over 300,000 graspable object models, precise 3D meshes, and accurate simulations to generate suitable grasping points. Additionally, the dataset includes real-world images for validation and quality control. Through simulated physics-based testing, over 13 million possible grasps were analyzed, including metrics for stability, force, and collision, to determine the most suitable grasp candidates. This dataset is available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/DexGraspNet. It has been successfully applied in a recent competition, outperforming other approaches with its state-of-the-art grasp detection results. Moreover, in an exhaustive search, it achieved an average success rate of 73% using stable grasps compared to 57% for other methods. However, it is essential to note that an exhaustive search is not suitable for real-world applications due to the significant computational requirements. Consequently, future work will involve the integration of learning-based grasp detection and planning methods to take full advantage of the dataset's capabilities. This is particularly important, as it has been observed that existing algorithms already benefit from using the dataset, with some showing a 10% improvement in performance when applied to the dataset alone. This suggests that future algorithms will likely see even greater benefits when specifically designed to utilize the dataset's extensive information. Ultimately, the development of dexterous robotic manipulation relies on the seamless integration of multiple AI techniques, and the dataset is poised to become an invaluable resource for driving further research in this area. It is anticipated that the dataset will continue to grow as more products are added, potentially expanding its scope to include other categories of objects. This will, in turn, facilitate the development of versatile robotic manipulation algorithms capable of applying their knowledge to a wide variety of objects beyond the initial dataset. This is particularly significant, given that the current dataset already encompasses over 300,000 products, and there are countless more available online. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements through parallel computing, leading to Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs) as a prominent solution. Asynchronous PEA execution, where evaluations are based on available computational time, causes fluctuating population sizes. This dynamic population results in an unfair distribution of time and resources among individuals, a bias known as evaluation time bias (ETB). Consequentially, individuals with better fitness might receive less opportunities to contribute their genetic material to the next generation. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a novel parent selection method, frequency-based selection (FBS), designed to mitigate the impact of evaluation time bias. FBS selects parents based on an individual's past selection frequency, thereby promoting diversity and ensuring that fitter individuals are selected more frequently. A comparative study was conducted between FBS and two established methods, random parent selection and proportional parent selection, demonstrating that FBS outperforms these methods in most scenarios and achieves comparable results in the remainder. Furthermore, experiments were carried out to evaluate the robustness of FBS in different computational environments and against a state-of-the-art multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, showing that FBS performs well in diverse settings. Notably, FBS outperforms random parent selection by 9.8% and is comparable to proportional parent selection in terms of mean quality, while also surpassing them by 10% in mean diversity. When paretoset-based metrics are used, FBS exhibits a 7% improvement over random parent selection and a 0.1% decline compared to proportional parent selection. Lastly, FBS is shown to be 8% more robust against changes in computational time than proportional parent selection and achieves a 100% survival rate in environments with varying computational time. When competing against the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II, FBS demonstrates a 4% improvement in mean quality, 8% in mean diversity, and a 6% in hypervolume metric. Notably, FBS is 8% more efficient than the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II in terms of mean function evaluations. network domain adaptation techniques, and the associated code is available on
GitHub at https://github.com/andre-veit/DeepNeuralNetworkDomainAdaptation.

hyperparameter, allowing it to adjust its explanation strategy as needed.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, has demonstrated superior performance in various machine learning tasks. In this letter, we investigate the potential of parallel training for LMU models on multi-gpu systems. Our findings suggest that parallel training for LMU can be realized by dividing the hidden state into separate gpu segments, resulting in a decentralized computation model. This decentralized approach can be applied to most standard loss functions, including which enables training using the Adam optimizer. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method and test its efficacy using the MNIST dataset, showcasing its ability to achieve comparable results to sequential training on single gpus. Moreover, our proposed method offers a significant time savings of approximately 65% with the addition of gpus, as well as a notable reduction in code complexity. Our experimental outcomes also reveal that parallel training for LMU can be safely applied across a wide range of network depths without compromising performance accuracy. Notably, the best-performing model among our experiments, a 7-layer LMU with 128 hidden units, achieved an impressive test accuracy of 98.04% on the MNIST dataset. This research provides a theoretical foundation for the development of more scalable deep learning systems, including the potential for model parallelism on large gpus or multi-gpu clusters. Furthermore, our proposed method can be extended to other types of recurrent neural networks, such as LSTMs, as a valuable contribution to the field. We anticipate that our research will inspire future investigations into the application of model parallelism for advanced RNNs like LMU. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/chenyilong85/parallel-lmu. Additionally, our research has been registered on arXiv as https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.15139. By building upon this work, we hope to foster a more collaborative research environment and encourage the sharing of knowledge with the deep learning community. PINN algorithms have achieved notable success in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite this advancements, PINNs often struggle with achieving accurate results for certain high-dimensional problems, largely due to the issue of spectral bias. This problem arises from the limited capacity of the neural network to approximate the complex target function, which can result in poor performance even with extensive data. This paper investigates the impact of training with momentum on mitigating spectral bias in PINNs, focusing specifically on a two-dimensional Poisson equation as the target function. The results indicate that incorporating momentum into the optimization process significantly improves the network's ability to approximate the target function, as evidenced by its enhanced performance using fewer data points and a smaller network. The momentum optimization variant is also shown to be more resilient to variations in hyperparameters such as data selection, network architecture, and loss function. The underlying reason behind this improvement is that momentum accelerates the network's initial rapid approximation of the target function's early low-frequency details, allowing it to better capture the high-frequency details subsequently. This advantage is expected to be more pronounced in higher-dimensional scenarios, where the target function's complexity increases with dimensionality. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for future investigations into the application of momentum and other forms of adaptive optimization for addressing spectral bias in PINNs, potentially extending to more complex, high-dimensional problems. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexanderstrathie/MomentumPINNs. The findings presented in this paper have been recognized with the 1st place finish in the NeurIPS 2022 Deep Learning for Materials Science Competition: Solving PDEs with PINNs. The winning work can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/understanding.

This type of problem, known as a minimax problem, has significant applications across various fields. To tackle this issue, we employ a constrained optimization approach and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality in the form of dual problems. Furthermore, we establish relationships between the optimality conditions of the minimax problem and those of a dual problem, specifically Fenton type minimax problems. Additionally, we investigate the problem of minimizing the maximum difference between two functions with a twist, namely, $\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}} \max_{0\leq x\leq 1} \sup_{y\in [0,1]} f(x-y) + g(y)$. In order to reduce this difficulty, this paper proposes a new approach by utilizing natural language descriptions that capture the program's intended behavior accurately and unambiguously. A new logic called Natural Hoare Logic (NHL) is introduced, which allows developers to create precise specifications by translating natural language descriptions into a formal language. By doing so, NHL makes it possible to apply traditional program verification techniques to ensure software correctness. An implementation of NHL has been developed and used to verify several programs, which demonstrates its feasibility and effectiveness in practice. The results show that NHL can effectively capture subtle program properties specified in natural language and provide sound and complete verification for imperative programs specified in Hoare logic. Moreover, NHL's expressiveness enables it to describe properties of total correctness, which goes beyond what is typically handled by Hoare logic, allowing for the expressiveness of separation logic and linear time complexity verification. An open-source tool has been created to support NHL, which includes a parser for logical forms, a model finder for satisfying assignments, and a proof automation tool for verifying program specifications. This paper presents a novel, deep graph neural networks (GCN) architecture that leverages a growing understanding of graph topology from coarse to detailed, allowing for efficient propagation of information. The architecture involves two main components: (1) a global pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton structure that progressively reduces input data resolution through a series of coarse-to-detailed feature propagations; and (2) a detailed topological link re-wiring mechanism that optimizes node connections and improves inter-node information exchange. We also release the code and dataset used in this study to facilitate future research. In the field of autonomous social agents, learning and adapting behaviors that consider the perspectives and actions of interacting entities is a significant challenge. We address this issue by introducing a model that utilizes transfer empowerment as a measure of intrinsic motivation to facilitate social learning and behavior. Our proposed algorithm detects opportunities for interaction based on differences in the agent's and partner's behavior, estimated using causal influence mapping. As a result, the agent learns to identify and respond to partner-specific actions, achieving transfer empowerment through consistent behavior in relevant situations. We validate the effectiveness of our approach using a variety of benchmarks, including a new benchmark designed to assess social learning and behavior. Compared to existing methods, our approach leads to more consistent and adaptable behaviors in both continuous and discrete domains. Additionally, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in learning and adapting behaviors in human-robot interaction tasks. Furthermore, our approach is found to be applicable in a real-world scenario, specifically in learning human-like behaviors in a robotic partner. Our research demonstrates that transfer empowerment can serve as a motivating factor for social learning and behavior, and we make our code available for public use. However, the gravitational influence on the Hawking temperature is more complex, as it is dependent on the location at which it is measured. chance to correct previous actions, resulting in a risk-averse approach often
utilized by advertisers. To mitigate uncertainty and protect their budgets, they
frequently set conservative bids, only to miss opportunities for more profitable
bids that remain unknown at the time of decision-making. Our solution involves an
adaptive bidding strategy that dynamically adjusts bids based on the relationship
between bid price and estimated auction value of completion, calculated using
data from previous auctions. By training this relationship on successful auctions,
where both bid and value are known, we employ a multi-objective optimization
technique that maximizes the difference between estimated value and bid while
minimizing the risk of not winning the auction and staying within budget.

accounted for in the budget. Our proposed method, dubbed ABRAC, demonstrates
superior performance to traditional risk-averse bidding in both synthetic and real-

Algorithmic interpretability refers to the clarity and ease with which a machine learning model can be understood by its human users. This proposed model views algorithmic interpretability as a measure of how efficiently and effectively humans learn algorithms. By applying this framework, we quantify the cognitive complexity of learning an algorithm as a unit of measurement to express its interpretability. This proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to various contexts, such as developers, operators, or deployers of an algorithm, allowing us to assess and compare the cognitive complexity of different groups under the same conditions. Furthermore, we present a practical example demonstrating how the proposed framework can be implemented to evaluate the cognitive complexity of a basic classification model. Our implementation, known as TiWS-iForest, achieves high detection efficiency at a relatively low cost, and we further enhance the algorithm's performance by pre-processing the data using a random forest. Through rigorous testing on public datasets, we evaluate the effectiveness of TiWS-iForest and compare its results to other one-traversal methods, demonstrating that it achieves high detection precision at a relatively low cost. Additionally, we showcase the application of TiWS-iForest in the context of wireless sensor networks within an airplane, highlighting its ability to accurately detect anomalies in real-time. Finally, we successfully deploy TiWS-iForest on 16 microcontrollers, verifying its feasibility in edge computing environments. The implementation of TiWS-iForest is publicly available on GitHub under the terms of the MIT license. We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is a necessary step in preparing data for scientific analysis and public release. Utilizing Herschel Space Observatory's archival data, the Hi-GAL survey aims to provide a uniform sub-millimeter wave catalog of the Galactic plane. Leveraging the reduced Herschel data from the Herschel Interactive Service for Astronomical Research (HISTAR), the pipeline enhances the quality of Hi-GAL Science Demonstration Phase (SDP) data. Comprising 50 square degrees at the Galactic plane's center, the SDP dataset serves as a test bed for pipeline validation. Additionally, we provide reduced data for the entire 420 square degree survey using Scan Map projection. This data is publicly accessible through the ESA Herschel Database (HiView). Finally, we outline plans for processing the remaining Observing Credit Allocations. Although Herschel is now decommissioned, the pipeline's products will remain relevant for future extragalactic surveys like the Herschel Astrophysical Terahertz Large Area Survey. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector representation, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm that locates potential matches within the database. This paper presents a new technique called active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, using a sampling strategy that prioritizes images likely to be closely related to the query. As a result, the same neural network can be combined with various indexing algorithms, and the sampling strategy can adapt to the strengths and weaknesses of each, leading to significant improvements in overall detection accuracy across different indexing methods, particularly for real-world images. Moreover, the proposed active indexing approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing image search pipelines and is readily applicable to other computer vision tasks, such as copy-paste detection and image retrieval. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of active indexing and outperform state-of-the-art techniques in various indexing methods, ultimately leading to a new state-of-the-art performance with a high recall rate of 94.4% on the CopyPASTE dataset. The high-$T_\textrm{c}$ superconducting state of cuprates exhibits a distinctive vortex-lattice phase that has been studied extensively in the past. Researchers have long debated the specific symmetry of this state, with some proposing that it might exhibit square-to-checkerboard ordering. To investigate this possibility, a team used local measurements of magnetic penetration depth via scanning SQUID microscopy to study the $H_{c2}$ phase transition in highly underdoped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.56}$ samples. By mapping the local $T_{c}$ transition under varying magnetic fields, they found evidence for a unique phase with local $T_{c}$ values distributed around a central temperature. This suggests the presence of a square-square vortex lattice transition, with the entire system transitioning at the average $T_{c}$ value and individual lattice points exhibiting slight variations due to local disorder. These findings provide the first direct observation of this specific phase transition and indicate that the square vortex-lattice phase is a universal feature in cuprate materials across a wide range of underdoping. Furthermore, the research shows that the square phase is characterized by homogeneous $T_{c}$ values, indicating that the system exhibits macroscopic electronic coherence at the critical temperature. Domain adaptation is a challenge where a model must adapt to a domain different from the one it was trained on. The'source-free' adaptation variant of this problem is distinct in that it prohibits access to the target domain's labeled data. Instead, the model can be cross-trained on unlabeled data from both the target domain and a separate training set. However, simply training this model on both domains results in overfitting due to differences between the two domains, and thus we propose Hypothesis Transfer, a method that involves training the model to make general predictions on the training set, and then using these general predictions to adapt to the target domain without needing target domain labels. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both unsupervised and semi-supervised adaptation tasks. The code for this method is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/chenkeye2020/SFHT. To study the atmospheric properties of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets, accurate extinction calculations are crucial, which necessitate reliable absorption data.  To address this need, a comprehensive database called EXOPLINES has been developed to provide absorption cross-sections for various molecular species relevant to cool atmospheres, spanning a broad temperature range from 500 to 2500K and covering wavelengths from 100 to 20000cm-1 (approximately 0.3 to 2.5μm). To facilitate this process, a list of 19 key molecules has been compiled, and their temperature-dependent properties, including molecular dissociation, ionization, and dimerization, as well as the resulting reaction rates and equilibrium constants, are taken into account. Our findings apply to broad categories of quantum theories, including more specific cases such as quantum deformed Markov categories. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the interplay between entropic quantities in thermodynamics can be generalized to the context of quantum resource theories, leading to the concept of a 'Legendre transform'. Our work also reveals that many known results in this field can be viewed as specific instances of more universal principles. As examples of the practical application of our results, we consider the cases of quantum interference, classical key interference and one-way classical communication. Our research provides a comprehensive mathematical framework for analyzing and better understanding the behavior of quantum systems governed by multiple constraints. Moreover, it offers a means of mapping entropic relationships in quantum resource theories onto their thermodynamic counterparts. Our work may inspire future studies on the interplay between quantum resources and thermodynamics. (Enhanced version of arXiv:2009.04493v3) (Originally published as arXiv:2009.04493)

To estimate hybrid measures like Renyi entropy and mutual information, we develop a method using a single set of statistical estimates obtained from a random variable's samples. By applying this approach to synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate its viability, specifically showing its applications in estimating mutual information between continuous random variables, detecting causal links in real-world data, and identifying independent random variables. The results indicate that our method is a strong alternative for estimating hybrid measures when compared to established alternatives. Notably, this work derives new formulas for estimating mutual information between continuous random variables, builds upon previous research by Deligiannlis et al. and Kotarachchi et al., and extends their scope to include Renyi and max-Renyi hybrid measures. Furthermore, we provide theoretical justifications for the method's reliability, including a proof that it can accurately estimate any measure with a finite number of moments. We investigate the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and boundary in higher-order topological insulators. Utilizing exact numerical calculations within the dynamical mean-field framework, combined with analytical modeling, we examine how bulk and boundary properties change in response to disorder. In the case of HgTe double layers with spin-orbit coupling, we find that disorder leads to a transition from a topological to an non-topological state, characterized by bulk and edge state bandgap closures. This transition is marked by a shift from mid-gap states at the interfaces to a band touching formed by disorder-activated bulk states and edge states. In contrast, for HgTe triple layers without spin-orbit coupling, our results reveal that disorder leads to a topological to non-topological phase transition characterized by bulk and edge state bandgap closures, and mid-gap states localized at the two interfacial boundaries rather than a single boundary edge mode. Furthermore, we demonstrate that disorder can induce a bulk and edge mode band touching similar to the Altland-Zirnbauer D class classification. Our findings provide a framework for understanding the disorder-induced topological phase transitions and offer insights into the bulk and boundary correspondence in complex disordered systems. To address this limitation, a novel deep learning-based approach to light field rendering has been developed, enabling novel views to be generated from sparse light field data collected using a single camera. This approach relies on two neural networks that learn to derive both depth information and novel view synthesis features from sparse data, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods that require access to full 4D light field datasets. Furthermore, our approach allows for extended light field rendering, incorporating additional warping and occlusion networks to accurately account for complex occlusion patterns in sparse data. The method was extensively evaluated on a range of publicly available light field datasets, yielding superior results and setting new benchmarks for light field rendering from sparse data. The associated code and pre-trained models can be found at https://github.com/alexander-martin/LightFieldNeuralRendering. Our approach has been successfully applied to novel view synthesis in computer vision and graphics, as well as to related applications such as virtual try-on and automotive driver assistance systems. field of view for the 4.07m SOAR telescope. Among the targets observed were 743 binaries,

ranges, and 251 without prior measurements. Additionally, 616 targets were studied to expand the 
record of measured separation ranges, and 0 new astronomical objects were identified. The median 
angular separations for the observed binaries fell within the 3.0 to 13.0 milliarcsecond range,

published new or updated information on 75% of the observed binaries, and 40% of the observed 
astrophysical objects overall. The results of these observations were presented in a series of 
papers, and the speckle interferometry data are accessible through the Center of Data at Universidade 
de São Paulo, and the Research Center for Speckle Astronomy at the University of Florida. The SOAR

Reinforcement learning strategies that make little to no assumptions about the environment's observability are often referred to as 'on-policy model-free methods.' These methods discover an estimate of the environment's dynamics through self-learning and utilize this understanding to learn policies directly from interactions. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) serve as a suitable framework for these scenarios, as they can simultaneously predict future observations using learned state representations. This study clarifies the connection between RNNs and recursive probabilistic belief updates in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). We demonstrate that RNNs, in their most basic form, learn a recursive parameterized representation of the environment's state distribution. We also provide a mathematical representation of the loss function for this state distribution, offering potential avenues for improvement. Additionally, our findings suggest that RNN-based methods can learn both the environment's dynamics and a state representation that facilitates efficient belief-updating. We support our theoretical analysis with experimental results, showing that simpler network architectures, as well as faster training times, can be achieved by leveraging the recursive structure of the environment's state distribution. We also observe that these benefits can be further amplified by adopting a variational inference approach, as it enables the efficient propagation of uncertainty through the environment's state distribution. Overall, our work sheds light on the theoretical underpinnings of model-free methods that employ RNNs, providing valuable insights for the design and analysis of these algorithms. We hope that our findings will inspire the development of more efficient model-free methods for partially observable environments. In video action recognition, fully-supervised learning methods that rely on dense annotations are resource-intensive and impractical due to the high cost of video labeling. However, the existing literature has revealed significant challenges in extending CH theory to games with multiple stages. To address these limitations, this study introduces a new class of such games, which allows for the derivation of a closed-form expression of the CH best response function. Our analysis demonstrates that the CH distribution in two-stage games differs substantially from its single-stage counterpart and exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with the parameter m, which represents the degree of self-awareness. Additionally, this study examines the properties of the CH best response function using theoretical and simulation-based methods, which enable the estimation of m values for specific games, such as the war of the models and the entry game. Our findings indicate that the m estimate for the war of the models is approximately 2, whereas it is around 0.5 for the entry game. Our empirical results show that the m estimate ranges from 2 for war of the models data to 0.5 for entry game data. A key advantage of using quantum machines could be in processing vast amounts of data, particularly through quantum versions of unsupervised and supervised learning. We've experimentally tested these concepts using a 14-qubit superconducting processor, initially applying unsupervised learning to create a binary classifier from raw data, and then using it to train an active learning strategy that selects specific training points. Our results show that quantum machines can tackle complex data analysis tasks, but currently face significant limitations due to errors in operation. By repeating experiments multiple times and averaging the results, we've managed to obtain accurate outcomes, and the quantum processor has indeed provided a processing speed advantage compared to its classical counterpart. However, full realization of quantum machine potential will require significant advances in device technology to reduce error rates, particularly when operating in bulk data settings. A crucial factor in text-to-speech synthesis is controlling the speech pitch, which the FastPitch model often struggles with. We developed and implemented a timbre-preservation technique, called TimbrePitch, to enhance pitch variability in speech synthesis. TimbrePitch starts by identifying a set of reference pitches for each desired pitch and then generates a corresponding set of timbre-matched embeddings for each reference pitch. We trained a mapping function to translate the target pitch embeddings to the mean embeddings of the reference pitches, allowing for the preservation of the speaker's distinct tone. To prevent changes to the speaker's tone altering the desired pitch, we added a constraint to the optimization process. Our experiments show that TimbrePitch significantly improves the quality of synthesized speech and increases the range of pitch variations while maintaining the natural tone of the speaker. Furthermore, incorporating TimbrePitch into FastPitch results in more natural and varied pitch inflections, outperforming previous approaches such as StyleTokens in pitch control. We also found that incorporating a timbre-matched mean pooling layer in the encoder improves the model's ability to synthesize speech at various pitches without compromising speech quality. Our research investigates the production of a $W$ boson paired with a $b\bar{b}$ pair in the context of standard model perturbation theory, focusing on the specific $pp\to W^{\pm}b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$ process at next-to-next-to-leading order. We develop a precise set of terms to match at next-to-leading order and derive corresponding Higgs-finite terms for the associated virtual corrections. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to leverage existing knowledge to accelerate the creation of new deep neural networks (DNNS). Transferability refers to the extent to which knowledge is shared between DNNS, with most studies focusing on understanding which DNNS can benefit from each other. However, the mechanisms by which DTL enhances performance have not been extensively explored, with many studies relying on simplified approximations. This paper challenges two widely accepted theories about transferability: that multi-task networks share knowledge and that similar datasets are transferable. By developing a novel method to quantify the impact of individual pre-trained models on target DNNS, we discovered that these theories do not always hold true. Instead, the extent to which knowledge is transferable depends on the specific nature of the tasks being performed by the pre-trained models, with attention to task-specific features being a key factor. Furthermore, we found that similar datasets are not necessarily transferable, with the key factor being the similarity in the features being attended to by the DNNS. These findings have significant implications for the design of DTL approaches, with the optimal strategy depending on the specific characteristics of the pre-trained models and target DNNS. Our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying DTL and offers practical guidance for practitioners. The efficiency of information and knowledge transfer across various social, technological, and biological networks is heavily influenced by their underlying structure.  The rate at which new information spreads within these networks depends on the initial conditions, with larger and more prominent nodes (influential individuals or key assets) receiving the information first.  As a measure of network organization, the modularity quantifies its inherent complexity and the resulting rate of information dissemination.  Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of both artificial and real-world networks, it has been found that an optimal level of modularity exists below which information transfer slows down and above which it accelerates due to over-dimensioning.  Consequently, network architects and managers can strategically design and manage these systems to optimize information transfer and the associated costs, with the modularity of the network's underlying architecture playing a pivotal role in the efficiency of information transfer and the associated costs.  This has significant implications for the management of complex systems and the design of efficient information transfer systems. Extremely large and complex models have achieved significant success in machine learning, despite their excessive capacity for complexity. A crucial factor contributing to this success is the ability of these models to find suitable representations through overparameterization, but the exact mechanisms driving this phenomenon are still not fully understood. This study investigates the connection between the computational requirements of finding global minima in convex optimization problems and the ability of overparameterized models to attain minimal errors. By considering the impact of specific assumptions regarding data distribution, loss function, and optimization algorithm, we establish a lower bound on the model size required to ensure minimal errors with high probability, under any given optimization method. Our results demonstrate that incorporating an accuracy constraint into the optimization process can relax this lower bound, and that this can be accomplished by leveraging the smoothness of the loss function. Furthermore, we show that incorporating a constraint on the number of gradient computations can also reduce the minimum required model size. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. Ultimately, our study provides a theoretical foundation for the empirical success of overparameterized models by linking it to computational constraints. By doing so, we shed light on the limitations of current optimization techniques and suggest potential improvements. Moreover, our results have implications for the understanding of the sample complexity of learning tasks. Finally, our study opens up new avenues of research related to the interplay between optimization, data acquisition, and model design. By considering the sample size as an additional constraint, we establish a new perspective on the trade-offs between model size and data requirements. This study is available in preprint form at arXiv-v2. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/andreabarbieri/overparameterization-from-computational-constraints.

This article's content builds upon a previous research, also published in Periodica Math. Hung., where a key finding demonstrated the non-existence of large Bohr sets within the context of countable abelian groups. By combining this result with an essential assumption stemming from an unpublished work by T. Tao, it can be conclusively shown that there are no two distinct subsets, denoted as $A$ and $B$, within a countable abelian group where both subsets possess a specific cardinality and a Bohr set formed by their sumset, respectively containing at least the power of $2^{\alpha}$ and $2^{\beta}$ elements while satisfying the condition that $\alpha + \beta < \frac{1}{5}$. This research further extends upon a challenge posed by Erdo's dual conjecture, specifically focusing on the non-existence of two distinct, sparse sets whose sumset generates a relatively dense Bohr set. By establishing a lower bound on the power of $p$, specifically $p \ge 2^{\frac{1}{5}}$, where this result holds true, it effectively addresses a challenge posed by an unpublished work by T. Tao. Lastly, it is also observed that this research's content is consistent with a more comprehensive finding, previously published by T. Tao in arXiv:0907.2523. Specifically, it is observed that the result can be generalized and that the power of $p$ can be replaced with a specific limit, denoted as $\lim_{\delta \to 0^+} \frac{1}{\log_2 \frac{1}{\delta}}$. A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential that ensures smooth, artifact-free evolution. However, determining the exact CD driving Hamiltonian can be complex and often impractical. We propose a variational approach to CD driving, where a parameter-dependent, effective Hamiltonian is approximated through a truncated expansion of the quantum circuit Hamiltonian's Taylor series. By iteratively optimizing a smaller, auxiliary circuit, this method yields a realistic, effective CD Hamiltonian that enables the preparation of target ground states with reduced computational complexity. Our results, obtained using the Hubbard model and full Gaussian theory, demonstrate that this method can produce high-fidelity CD driving with minimal supporting potential and, consequently, rapid state preparation. The method's potential applications in preparing complex, multi-qubit states and simulating real materials are also discussed. Data envelopment analysis relies on the development of a production frontier, a task often approached with parametric or non-parametric methods utilizing either discrete or flexible regression techniques. As a middle ground, non-convex but convex relaxations present an alternative strategy, specifically with the use of the StoNED procedure introduced by Kneip et al. in 2016. This method, based on a series of conditional distribution functions, leads to the application of a convex optimization problem, a process that can be computationally demanding. In response, a Python package called pyStoNED has been created to streamline the application of the StoNED procedure through the use of NumPy and Quandl libraries, also incorporating an efficient implementation based on the CVXPY solver. The package's capabilities are demonstrated through its application in the analysis of stock returns and S&P 500 index data. Additionally, a comprehensive R package, also a convex optimization-based implementation known as RStoNED, was developed concurrently by another researcher. In comparison, the pyStoNED package is found to be faster and more memory-efficient than its RStoNED counterpart, achieving a speed-up of approximately 75% and a corresponding reduction in memory usage of around 85%. This performance disparity is attributed to several key factors, specifically the inherent advantages of Python over R, the superiority of NumPy's array operations, the benefits of using the CVXPY solver, as well as the drawbacks associated with R's interpretive nature and the limitations imposed by RStoNED's C++ implementation. In contrast, the use of a just-in-time compiler like PyPy is found to have a negligible impact on the computational efficiency of the pyStoNED package. Ultimately, the pyStoNED package is intended to facilitate the adoption of the StoNED procedure among researchers and practitioners, a goal that is also shared by the RStoNED package in tandem. One feasible approach to achieving standardization is through a process called inverse text normalization (ITN), which involves normalizing written quantities into numerical values and has proven effective when trained with large datasets. However, ITN's performance can be hindered by factors such as limited data availability and data inconsistencies. This study delves into the challenges associated with ITN and proposes a data enhancement technique to address them. By utilizing a generator that introduces ITN-related errors, we demonstrate that ITN models can be trained on artificially created data, resulting in improved performance. This method is particularly effective in scenarios with limited natural data and is adaptable to various neural network architectures. Experimental results on a German dataset indicate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in numerical value extraction and data augmentation. Moreover, we also introduce a new dataset augmentation method for ITN, which involves generating artificial data by modifying the written numerical forms to create new instances. This new method outperforms existing techniques and sets a new benchmark for ITN and future research. A comprehensive study using $NpT$ MD simulations has been conducted to compare the residual entropy and viscosity of various model potentials with corresponding real-world molecular fluids, specifically ethane and carbon disulfide. The binary potentials of Vijazala et al. were used to mimic the molecular interactions, with the high temperature model exhibiting a soft repulsive nature and the low temperature model featuring a much stiffer repulsive potential. It was discovered that the viscosity of the binary potentials aligns with the corresponding non-associated fluid model of ethane and carbon disulfide, respectively, across a broad temperature scope. However, the high temperature model outperformed the low temperature model of ethane and carbon disulfide at low temperatures. The study also found that the effective number of freedom for the binary potentials and the ethane model via $NVE$ simulations is directly linked to the binary potentials' temperature-dependent parameter, $\tau$. Furthermore, the study suggests that the effective number of freedom for carbon disulfide cannot be captured by the binary potential approach. Lastly, the study found that the viscosity of the binary potentials is influenced by the residual entropy, indicating a reciprocal relationship between the two properties. Specifically, the study found that the high friction regime exhibits a direct relationship and the low friction regime exhibits an inverse relationship. The study's findings provide valuable insights into the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity, serving as a crucial step in the development of novel force fields that accurately predict both properties. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics, invariant-set theory, proposes that quantum particles reside on a set-defined space, where their pre-quantum history is examined using a complex mathematical framework. This paper investigates the mathematical underpinnings of the theory by exploring the properties of the given complex space and develops a hidden-variable model based on a specific simplified representation of this space. Our analysis reveals that, when represented in this simplified form, the quantum state can be expressed as a function of these hidden variables, aligning with the requirements of a hidden-variable model. Furthermore, our results suggest that, when considering the entire invariant set, the probability distributions associated with standard quantum mechanics can be viewed as conditional probabilities, given this underlying set of hidden variables. This paper also examines the implications of assuming that hidden variables exist and discusses the constraints they must satisfy to produce the observed quantum statistics. Our analysis ultimately reveals that, when represented in this simplified form, the quantum state exhibits pathological behavior, failing to match the predictions of quantum mechanics with sufficient precision, even for large sets of hidden variables. This outcome casts doubt on the potential of invariant-set theory as a viable superdeterministic modification to the foundations of quantum mechanics. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage. (iii) an adaptable architecture that accommodates various IoTs with differing CPU power levels. Our proposed CNN outperforms existing solutions like DeepSignal and CASSANDRA, achieving a comparable 98.3% accuracy with 97% fewer multiplications and 59% fewer parameters. The Compact CNN model also boasts exceptional efficiency, executing in 230ms with 14KB memory on a Raspberry Pi 3 A+ and in 10ms with 1.7KB memory on an ESP32. Our code is available at https://github.com/andreabaccan/CCNN.

We investigate the challenge of developing controllers that can adapt to unpredictable changes in dynamic systems. Continual Learning, a machine learning subfield, demands learning an accumulation of skills and abilities from a series of tasks, with each task's data and labels being accessed sequentially. The traditional method of training on each task separately results in performance degradation when applied to subsequent tasks. Various online continual learning approaches have been developed to process tasks sequentially without knowledge preclusion, but they often struggle with knowledge retention. This paper presents a novel framework, NEOL, which incorporates online distillation to enhance both short-term and long-term knowledge retention. Experimental results across multiple datasets and models demonstrate that NEOL achieves a significant 9.86% improvement in overall accuracy compared to the next best method, with a notable 100% improvement in some cases when compared to the baseline method. The source code for NEOL is publicly available at https://github.com/uta-srl/NEOL. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art continual learning techniques, including online distillation, online fine-pruning, and elastic learning methods, with results showing a 5.98% average improvement in accuracy and 40.52% in some cases when compared to the best existing method. The comprehensive comparison of continual learning techniques and our method's performance is documented at https://uta-srl.github.io/NEOL. The knowledge graphs used in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/uta-srl/NEOL/tree/main/data. The pre-trained models obtained from this research are publicly available at https://github.com/uta-srl/NEOL/tree/main/checkpoints. In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{h}$ where the prime $p$ is two or an odd number. Furthermore, we present several families of sparse permutation polynomials in the form of $x^{q+1}+A$ over finite fields with cube orders, with the coefficients $A$ expressed as power sums of the coordinates of the variable $x$. Lastly, we propose several types of APN and LPS functions over finite fields with cube orders, with the formats $f(x)+g(T(x))$ and $f(x)+\mathrm{Tr}_{q^{3}/q}(x^{q+1})$, where the functions $f$ and $g$ are permutation and affine respectively. These results provide the foundation for the construction of different types of APN and LPS ciphers. Additionally, we present several instances of complete permutation polynomials of various degrees in three variables over finite fields with cube orders, with the aim of enhancing the performance of the differential attack and reducing the LPS differential probability. Finally, we present several instances of complete permutation polynomials of various degrees in four variables over finite fields with cube orders, with the aim of enhancing the performance of the linear attack and reducing the LPS linearity. The results of the paper are presented in the forms of tables and figures. These results provide the foundation for the construction of different types of lightweight block and stream ciphers.
