The method's results are also compared to those obtained by human annotators, and while some discrepancies are found, the method's performance is generally close to human standards. The research also identifies areas where further improvement is needed and suggests potential solutions to address these limitations. The method's efficiency is further demonstrated through its application to a series of satellite images covering over 2000 square kilometers in the Amazon rainforest, and the results are made available to support ongoing research in this critical ecosystem. The method's performance is also compared to that of a state-of-the-art deep learning-based approach, and while some differences are found, the results indicate that the method is generally comparable or even superior in certain aspects. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a critical component in diagnosis, research, and clinical care. Current automated methods face challenges due to their training on data from a single hospital, which can lead to overfitting and difficulties with adaptation to new, unseen data. A potential solution to this problem is parameter-efficient tuning, which involves adjusting only the most critical model parameters. In this paper, we investigate the feasibility of modifying the model's special token, initially set to represent input IDs, to serve as a key for decoding and pre-training purposes. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that merges the two models and propose a new optimization technique for the resulting combined operation. Our findings suggest that the incorporation of context can substantially influence preference rankings in multi-set addition operations, and a more detailed understanding of these preferences may be essential to accurately identify the optimal solution in such cases. Our goal is to develop a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between thermodynamics and dynamics in the development of glass-forming polymer fluids, with a focus on the early stages of cooling. Through detailed simulations, we investigate how the configurational entropy of these fluids changes in response to slow cooling for various model systems. The dynamics of these changes are examined using the concept of configurational entropy density and the configurational entropy relaxation time, both of which are crucial indicators of a system's stability and its propensity to form glass. The interplay between thermodynamics and dynamics is studied through the relationship between configurational entropy and its relaxation time, with a particular focus on identifying normal and supercooled liquids. The observed dynamics are consistent with a non-Arrhenius temperature dependence of the configurational relaxation time, with a specific exponent that varies depending on the strength of interactions within the polymer chains. The observed behavior is explained by considering the complexity of glass-forming polymer fluids, with a model based on the mode coupling theory providing a coherent understanding of these results. The applicability of this theoretical framework is further supported by comparing our simulation results with available experimental data for a real-world polymer fluid. In neural machine translation, the attention model is critical to NMT system performance. However, its current design has a limitation: an encoder-to-predictor attention profile that follows a sequential order. This paper presents an alternative, called look-ahead attention, which allows the NMT model to consider relationships between target tokens appearing later in the sequence. Our experiments on the IWSLT'15 English-to-German and WMT'16 English-to-German datasets indicate that look-ahead attention leads to notable gains in test BLEU scores, with improvements of 0.8 and 1.1 points observed in the mentioned datasets, respectively. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis reveals that look-ahead attention is particularly beneficial when the source language is complex and there are many late-time target words in the translation. Our findings suggest that incorporating look-ahead attention is a valuable strategy for enhancing NMT system performance. A crucial factor in understanding the magnetic field generation in astrophysical objects and their behavior is the role of turbulence. Mean-field theory combined with its back effect principle offers a framework to describe complex magnetic field dynamics, yet it relies on a simplified representation of turbulent effects. By employing a novel, highly detailed mean-field representation, our study shows that these simplifications can lead to substantial inaccuracies, particularly when modeling the complex dynamics of global convective dynamos, where a broad range of turbulent effects is at play. Our results suggest that these dynamos are inherently unstable and produce highly irregular magnetic field configurations, even when using a simplified representation of turbulence, in contrast to predictions of stable solutions and smooth patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these irregularities deepen and create more complex structures as the resolution of the simulation increases, indicating that these dynamos are inherently non-linear and highly sensitive to their environment. Due to the dynamic nature of radio frequency energy, identifying these interferences can be a complex task, particularly in shared wireless networks where high-bandwidth applications may generate interference in other parts of the spectrum. This study proposes a method for identifying multiple wireless interferences using a device's spectrum analyzer readings and applies it to data obtained from a 2.4 GHz wireless local area network. By training a convolutional neural network, the method can automatically detect and identify interferences without the need for prior knowledge of their characteristics. Notably, our approach can identify and classify multiple wireless interferences simultaneously, a capability that complements existing interference identification techniques. Moreover, our results demonstrate that this method can be successfully applied to both indoor and outdoor environments and remains effective even when the interference signal is weak compared to the desired wireless signal. Ultimately, this method has the potential to be integrated into spectrum analyzer devices as a valuable tool for identifying wireless interferences in real-world applications. Experimental findings indicate that the method achieves an impressive accuracy of over 90% in identifying interferences. Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, research has shown that even experienced developers often fail to maintain high-quality test code, with poorly written tests causing significant issues down the development pipeline. To address this issue, researchers have been studying test quality through the lens of test smells, identifying and quantifying indicators of suboptimal test code. While previous studies have explored the prevalence and impact of test smells, an empirical investigation into developers' perceptions of test smells as quality indicators has not been conducted. In this study, we aimed to bridge this knowledge gap by gathering the opinions of professional developers on the severity of six test smells, utilizing a mixed-methods approach that combined both quantitative and qualitative research methods. Our findings reveal that developers' subjective assessments of test smells as quality indicators can diverge significantly from objective evidence of their impact on test code. Notably, developers tend to overestimate the severity of smells that are easily identifiable and underestimate the severity of those that are harder to detect. Our research highlights the importance of a dual perspective on test smells, combining both developer perspectives and objective measures to refine and adapt smell detection and refactoring strategies. Additionally, our findings suggest that developers' perceptions of smell severity can serve as an effective basis for guiding refactoring efforts, rather than solely relying on objective metrics. Finally, our study provides valuable insights for improving the effectiveness of test quality improvement initiatives, particularly those targeting specific smells, by taking into account the perspectives of software developers. Our research offers practical recommendations for practitioners and researchers, emphasizing the need to involve developers in the development of smell detection and quality metrics, and to consider the impact of smell visibility on its perceived severity. By acknowledging that smell severity is a subjective quality that can vary across individuals, we can develop more tailored approaches to improving test quality, ultimately leading to better quality software. Our research opens up new avenues for investigation, such as exploring the impact of experience and domain expertise on perceptions of smell severity, and the relationship between smell severity and post-release bug counts. By understanding the complex interplay between developer perceptions and objective measures of smell impact, we can develop more comprehensive and effective strategies for detecting and preventing smells. Our study contributes to the software quality body of knowledge by shedding light on the relationship between developer perceptions and objective measures of smell impact, and by providing practical recommendations for improving smell detection and quality metrics. Our research offers valuable insights for researchers working in the software quality domain, particularly those focusing on testing and software quality

In this paper, we investigate the use of a more robust contrasting approach based on optimal transportation, specifically the Sinkhorn distance, to address these limitations. Additionally, we derive an analytical proof demonstrating that the learned embedding converges to an optimal solution, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of DSE in comparison to state-of-the-art deep metric learning methods on a range of benchmark datasets. Data analysis applications such as topological data analysis demand efficient algorithms for Betti numbers of extreme value trajectories. Prior studies have examined Betti numbers in the dense case, but this work delves into the sparse scenario where the sample size and dimension grow at the same rate. We investigate the Betti numbers of one-dimensional extreme value samples and demonstrate that under certain conditions on the sample size and sample path properties, the expected values converge to the values obtained from the associated Gaussian fields, provided the sample size grows at least as $\epsilon^{-2}$, where $\epsilon$ represents the local dimension. This growth rate is identical to the dense sampling regime, yet significantly lower than the previous sparse sampling regime found in the literature. We also examine the convergence of variance for the zeroth Betti number and reveal that it converges to infinity as the sample size grows. Building upon these findings, we extend our analysis to higher-dimensional extreme value samples and establish similar asymptotic results. Our methodology involves applying the principles of extreme value theory and topological data analysis, and is supported by numerical simulations. These simulations align with our theoretical predictions and provide insight into the asymptotic behavior of Betti numbers. Our research appears to be the first comprehensive study on the asymptotic properties of Betti numbers in the sparse sampling regime, and is based on novel technical contributions that may be of independent interest. We leverage the concept of $\beta$-connected components, a novel topological structure that enables efficient computation and further analysis. Our computational approach is grounded in the application of persistence diagrams and the computation of expected persistence diagrams through Monte Carlo simulations. This work is accompanied by a publicly accessible Python code repository that includes the implementation of the numerical simulations and the computation of the expected persistence diagrams. This code is available at the following URL: https://github.com/andreabarbieri/persistent-betti-numbers. Our research has been further extended in the paper titled "Efficient Computation of Betti Numbers for Gaussian Excursions via Stochastic Continuation", where we present a novel algorithm for the efficient computation of Betti numbers. This algorithm is based on the application of the persistence diagrams and the computation of the expected persistence diagrams through a stochastic continuation approach. Our computational results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, and we anticipate that it will be of significant interest to the topological data analysis community. A publicly accessible Python code repository that includes the implementation of the computational results is available at the following URL: https://github.com/andreabarbieri/betti

We propose an innovative method for calibrating an eye-in-hand camera setup
utilizing a single 2D image. Our approach requires prior knowledge of the robotic
arm's pose in 3D space and relies on identifying corresponding features in
both the 2D image and the subsequent 3D scene model. To achieve this, we employ
a deep learning-based technique to predict 3D coordinates for these features
in the image. Our algorithm then generates a set of camera views and uses them
to build a 3D model of the environment. Once the 3D model is constructed, we
use the known robotic arm poses to create a set of corresponding 2D images and
3D features, allowing us to calculate the necessary transformation parameters
for the eye-in-hand camera setup. Our approach was successfully tested using
the NYU Depth V2 dataset and compared to existing methods. Our results indicate
that our method can achieve comparable accuracy with a more conventional two-step
process, but at a significant cost reduction by avoiding the need for additional
images. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/utias-stacked/eihc-from-image.

Current methods primarily focus on node-level data poisoning and rely on specific attack strategies, limiting their adaptability to various real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present a novel data poisoning attack on GNNs that utilizes reinforcement learning to optimize the selection of vulnerable nodes to target. A hypergraph is said to possess bounded expansion if a certain sequence of values in the hypergraph's complexity has the smallest possible growth rate, where the complexity is a measure of the hypergraph's size. Domain-specific knowledge is often represented using ontologies, which are complex, hierarchical knowledge graphs. Visualising all the connections between concepts can be challenging due to their interconnected structure. In this paper, an innovative visualisation method, OntoPlot, is introduced to effectively display non-hierarchical relationships among a subset of closely related concepts within large, hierarchical ontologies. OntoPlot's unique circular layout helps to preserve the initial classification system's visibility, while also highlighting novel insights gained from exploring these associated concepts. A user-friendly interface enables seamless navigation, and when interacting with the visualisation, related hierarchical and non-hierarchical information can be easily accessed. OntoPlot's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to two domain-specific ontologies, with a publicly accessible prototype available online. A novel joint framework for machine translation and parsing is proposed, incorporating a new decoding algorithm inspired by top-down parsing methods. This approach builds upon existing work by incorporating a non-projective parsing algorithm, eliminating sentence-level decisions through sentence mean field inference, and utilizing syntactic connections to guide word-by-word decoding. Furthermore, the framework's ability to identify correct parsing structures and mitigate the issue of overly complex parsing in the English-German dataset is observed. To accurately determine the binding energies of molecules, it's essential to consider various factors such as the interactions with ice surfaces, solvent effects, and energy distributions. However, there's a lack of a unified database that provides comprehensive information on the binding energies of molecules, particularly in the astrochemical community. To address this gap, we've developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEP), a web-based database that collects and shares quantum chemical binding energy distributions, as well as experimental and theoretical binding energies of molecules related to astrochemistry. The platform allows users to search for specific molecules and their binding energies with respect to water, ice, and other relevant substrates, providing access to a wide range of data, including energy distributions, mean binding energies, and desorption energies. The platform also facilitates the comparison of binding energies with respect to different factors, such as temperature and surface coverage, and includes a discussion forum for users to share their research findings and engage in scientific discussions. The BEP is an essential resource for the astrochemical community, providing a comprehensive database of binding energies and facilitating the sharing of data and knowledge among researchers. The platform's database currently contains over 5000 binding energy data points, including experimental and theoretical values, and is expected to continue growing as a valuable resource for astrochemists in the future. A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a geometric Brownian motion serves as a baseline, but with a twist: the natural exponentiation may result in a value that falls below a certain threshold $\epsilon$, in which case the next iteration is set to $\epsilon$ instead. This process finds practical use in scenarios where growth cannot be negative, and its properties are examined through both theoretical and numerical analyses, including a case study on how these stochastic processes can facilitate the modeling of population dynamics. A discrete-time equivalent of this process is also explored, and a discrete-time model is developed to simulate the dynamics of a single population subject to density-dependent growth, Allee effects, and random environmental fluctuations, with the goal of identifying the conditions that allow a population to successfully recover from the brink of extinction. This investigation is informed by a diverse set of real-world applications, including human populations, insect swarms, cancer cells, and social media followers. The analysis reveals that the stochastic process with the lower bound can serve as an effective model for studying the dynamics of a single population, and it provides valuable insights into the conditions that enable a population to avoid extinction. This includes the necessity of achieving a certain population size, rather than the average growth rate, and the importance of finding an optimal balance between these factors. These findings are further supported by a series of numerical simulations that demonstrate how the model can be used to forecast the future population sizes based on a set of model parameters, and they are shown to be consistent with a range of empirical observations, including a study on the resilience of cancer cells in the presence of targeted therapy. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that the stochastic process with the lower bound can serve as a valuable tool for modeling population dynamics, and it provides a range of applications that extend far beyond the scope of this specific case study. As a result, it is anticipated that this process will find a wide range of applications in modeling and analyzing multiplicative stochastic processes in various disciplines. Furthermore, the investigation into the conditions that allow a population to successfully recover from the brink of extinction can be extended to a broader set of systems and phenomena, including nonlinear stochastic processes, and it is anticipated that the results of this research will have a significant impact on our understanding of the dynamics of real-world systems. Finally, the analysis highlights the importance of leveraging mathematical and computational tools to develop and test models of complex systems, and it is anticipated that the results of this research will inspire future investigations into the modeling and analysis of multiplicative stochastic processes. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' Theorem established that ex(n, F) equals (1 alpha(F))n^2, where 0 <= alpha(F) <= 1, for sufficiently large n. In 1973, Erdos posed a question about determining alpha(F) for specific graphs. In 2018, Erdos asked a similar question for single hypergraph F = F_r, consisting of a single r-uniform hyperedge [u_1, u_2,..., u_r] where u_1 < u_2 <... < u_r. This paper provides an explicit value of alpha(F_r) for all r uniform hypergraphs F_r, proving it equals 1/r. The proof involves constructing an F_r-free r-uniform graph G on r^2 vertices with maximum edges. The graph G can be described as a complete bipartite multigraph (A, B) with |A| = |B| = r and weights a_i for the elements in A and b_i for the elements in B. The condition that the sum of a_i minus b_i is not equal to 0 ensures that G is F_r-free. The construction of this graph and its weight distribution allows us to derive the value of alpha(F_r). The same approach can be used to determine the Lagrangian density for more general hypergraphs. The authors also provide a precise formula for the maximum number of a-factors in an r-uniform graph on n vertices. The study of these problems is motivated by their connection to the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz and the Generalized Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. The results of this paper can be seen as a hypergraph analogue of the findings in the paper 'An irrational Lagrangian density of a complete graph' by the same authors. The authors also provide an alternative interpretation of the problem and its solution using tensor products and matrix pencils. The solution to the problem and its variations has been successful in an r=2 case as shown by the authors' previous work. The analysis is further supported by a thorough discussion of its practical implications and a comparative review of its similarities and differences with the existing literature. Lastly, a numerical example is presented to demonstrate the model's capabilities in describing phenomena such as heat waves and fronts. Creating reliable automatic tools for analyzing COVID-19, a disease caused by the coronavirus, is crucial due to its widespread nature and the need for rapid diagnosis. Medical professionals rely on computer-aided detection and segmentation tools to accurately detect lung lesions and distinguish between COVID-19, adenocarcinoma, and other types of pulmonary diseases. However, developing effective detection and segmentation tools is challenging due to the small size of lung lesions and the need for accurate data annotation. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that utilizes weakly supervised learning to accurately locate and segment COVID-19-related lesions. By treating image-level annotations as hidden variables, we develop an end-to-end model that optimizes segmentation and classification. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in lesion detection and segmentation, achieving a 79.44% increase in dice similarity coefficient, and demonstrates competitive performance in classification, with a 94.1% classification accuracy. Additionally, our approach enables the detection of smaller lesions, resulting in a 50% reduction in mean bounding box area compared to state-of-the-art methods. Vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications. 1) The traditional method relies on manual input which is time-consuming and prone to errors. 2) The state-of-the-art deep learning-based approaches demand significant human annotation. This paper presents a fully automatic pipeline for identifying and positioning vertebras on unannotated CT scans. Firstly, we use a novel technique to correct and straighten the spine in three dimensions. Then, vertebras are identified using a new method that takes into account anatomical constraints and considers the variability of vertebrae shapes. The proposed pipeline demonstrates high accuracy, achieving a 97.5% and 96.8% success rate in identifying individual vertebras and thoracic/cervical lumbar levels respectively. Additionally, it demonstrates strong robustness, with a 95% success rate even when the input images are distorted. The proposed pipeline outperforms existing solutions in terms of accuracy, while maintaining simplicity and requiring minimal user calibration. The code and data used in this research are openly accessible on the repository https://github.com/ChenXinyu1995/Vertebra_Loc_Identifier. The primary goal of fashion image retrieval involves identifying matching images 
with varying attributes, such as gender, clothing items, and accessories. 
However, existing methods are hindered by their inability to manipulate attributes 
at the feature level, which is crucial for accurate retrieval. To address this issue, 
we introduce a novel framework for semi-supervised feature-level attribute manipulation. 
Our approach consists of two key components: a cross-distribution attribute translation 
module that learns attribute information from annotated data, and a self-learning 
feature adaptation module that extracts feature information from unlabeled data. 
By leveraging semi-supervised learning, we enhance our framework's robustness using 
a co-training discriminator. Experimental results on the FashionAI dataset demonstrate 
its superior performance compared to baseline methods in retrieving images with 
specific attributes after manipulation. Code implementation available at https://github.com/your-username/FI-RL.

This research introduces a dynamic programming approach, the dual gradient flow, for resolving linear ill-posed problems within the context of Banach spaces. Leveraging a virtual source condition, a regularized problem is formulated as a constrained optimization issue. A key innovation lies in replacing the constraint qualification with a logarithmic term, enabling the analysis of raw Banach space sequences without introducing additional assumptions. Subsequently, a discrete dynamical system, the dual gradient flow, is constructed to approximate the optimal solution of the optimization problem. Furthermore, a convergence result for the numerical method is established under minimal assumptions on the data. Lastly, the method's efficacy is demonstrated through a variety of numerical experiments. In particular, the method is applied to the solution of the inverse source problem for the heat equation. The results show that the method can accurately determine the location and intensity of the heat source even when only limited and noisy data are available. In addition, the method is used to investigate the solution of the inverse coefficient problem for the Laplace equation. The results reveal that the method can effectively determine the coefficient under various types of boundary conditions. The numerical methods developed in this research are versatile and can be applied to a broader range of problems in functional analysis. The research also provides a theoretical foundation for the use of gradient flows in the solution of ill-posed problems and opens up new avenues for the extension of the methods to the solution of nonlinear problems.
